title: The family of churches, looking back
tomorrow: is there anything that can come between you and God?

lines: A CHANT, A HYMN, A GOSPEL CHOIR.
cards: Three choirs in one room. One chants, low and steady, the way Orthodox choirs often do. One sings an old Latin hymn.
One is a gospel choir that can't keep still. On paper it sounds like a mess. In the room, if they listen to each other, it sounds like a chord.
That's the family of churches this path has visited: Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant, many rooms, one house.

teach.b: Paul gives the picture, writing to a church in Corinth that was splitting into camps, each claiming a favorite teacher.
“For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.”

teach.h: I HAVE NO NEED OF THEE? NO.
teach.b: Then the line to tell a friend: “And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee.” Not one sound. Many, needing each other.
The family has real voices. Orthodox Christians, with icons, incense and the Divine Liturgy. Catholic Christians, with the Mass, the saints and the pope.
Protestant Christians, in many churches, with the Bible read and preached and hymns sung together. They differ on real things, and they say so: communion, authority, Mary and the saints.
Naming those differences honestly is part of loving one another, not a failure of it. And they share real things too.

teach.h: ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.
teach.b: Paul names some in one breath: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.”
On his last night, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for everyone who will believe later, “That they all may be one.” That prayer is still being prayed in all three rooms.

how: Christians of different churches pray for unity in their own services, and some gather across churches to pray and sing together, often using Jesus's words in John 17.

games.q: what does “the family of churches” mean?
o: a list of churches that agree on everything
one church that replaced all the others
Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant, one family

p: the Mass, the saints, the pope
one Lord, one faith, one baptism

s: unity between churches means they agree on everything
they differ on communion, authority, Mary and the saints, and say so. unity there sounds like harmony.
Paul says the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee
one body, many members, needing each other.
'in my Father's house are many mansions' is about different churches
Jesus was speaking of where he was going. 'many rooms' is a picture, not his meaning.

games.q: at a wedding, the bride's Orthodox family and the groom's Baptist family each want their own customs. what fits Paul's picture of the body?
o: pick one family's way, so nobody gets confused.
keep both, with the differences named honestly: one body, many members.
drop every church custom so there's no difference at all.
games.why: the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee. one body keeps its many members, and needs each.

practice: Listen for one minute to the sounds around you: a fan, a car, a bird, a voice in another room. Pick them out one by one, and notice how they sit together without becoming one sound.
If you pray, pray for the churches by name as the sounds go on: Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant; if not, hold them in mind with good will.

wordCard.voice: The family of churches. Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant Christians: real differences, one Lord, one body with many members.

orig.note: the Greek for 'may be one' in John 17:21.

carryVoice: Your line: that they may be one. Many voices, one chord: harmony, not unison. See you tomorrow.
